basics: The hand is built in three tiers: the wrist (carpals), the palm (metacarpals) and the fingers (phalanges). The wrist is not one hinge but a cluster of eight small, roughly cube-shaped bones packed in two rows of four and lashed together by ligaments, so wrist motion is the sum of many small slides between bones. Names are read with the hand in anatomical position (palm forward, thumb outward), so 'lateral' means the thumb side and each row is listed thumb-to-little-finger. The proximal row sits against the forearm; of its four bones only the scaphoid and lunate actually meet the radius to form the wrist joint proper, and the ulna is kept off the carpals by a fibrocartilage disc. The distal row meets the metacarpals. Each name is a shape: boat, moon, three-cornered, pea, four-sided figures, head-shaped, hooked. The slide leaves unsaid that the scaphoid is the bone that most often breaks in a fall, because load passes capitate to scaphoid to radius.

basics: This is the palm-side (anterior) view of a right hand, so the radius and thumb are on the left of the picture and the little-finger side on the right. Read the rows from the radius outward: proximal row scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, with the pea-shaped pisiform sitting on the front face of the triquetrum, which is why it stands out from this side; distal row trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate. The capitate is the largest carpal and its rounded head fits into the lunate. The hook of the hamate and the pisiform on one side, and the scaphoid and trapezium on the other, form the raised walls of a shallow trough on the palm; a fibrous band roofs it to make the carpal tunnel, through which the finger-flexing tendons and the median nerve pass. The line labelled carpometacarpal joint is where the distal row meets the bases of the five metacarpals. Unsaid: the thumb's joint with the trapezium is what lets it swing across the palm.

basics: The foot is laid out like the hand: a block of short bones at the back (seven tarsals versus the wrist's eight), five long metatarsals in the middle, and fourteen phalanges in the toes, the big toe (hallux) having only two. The slide is a view from above. The talus is the keystone, the only foot bone that touches the leg. Its pulley-shaped top (trochlear surface) is gripped between the two ankle knobs (malleoli) of the tibia and fibula; that grip is the ankle joint. Weight coming down the tibia lands on the talus and splits: about half goes back to the calcaneus, the largest tarsal, whose rear tuberosity is the heel; the rest goes forward through the navicular, three wedge-shaped cuneiforms and cube-shaped cuboid into the metatarsals. Each metatarsal and phalanx has a base, body and head; the first metatarsal is thickest as it carries most load. Unsaid on the slide: these bones form springy arches held by ligaments and tendons, which absorb shock at each step.

terms.d: The ankle region of the foot: the seven tarsal bones.

A large rough bump on a bone for a tendon or ligament attachment; on the calcaneus, the heel point.
Wedge-shaped; the three cuneiform tarsals sit in a row between the navicular and metatarsals 1 to 3.
The bony knob on each side of the ankle: medial malleolus on the tibia, lateral malleolus on the fibula.
